paragraphs: Logic synthesis simplifies a circuit while preserving what it computes. Many synthesis heuristics work through a graph representation of the circuit, trying transformations on smaller regions. The authors find that many attempted transformations accomplish little, yet still consume computation. They identify Resub and Mfs2 as heuristics whose execution often accounts for much of the total optimization time.

PruneX introduces a learned way to reduce these ineffective transformation attempts. Its central challenge is generalization: a predictor useful on circuits encountered during training must also work on unfamiliar circuits. The proposed framework uses knowledge that remains valid under circuit transformations to learn representations intended to remain useful across circuit domains. This makes transfer to unseen designs a central part of the method.

The authors integrate PruneX into Resub and Mfs2 and evaluate it on industrial and very large circuits. They report runtime improvements of up to 3.1 times while maintaining comparable optimization performance. The finding supports using learned screening to accelerate existing synthesis heuristics without requiring a corresponding sacrifice in the circuit improvements achieved in those experiments.
icml-2024-a-circuit-domain-generalizatio.tldr: PruneX learns to reduce ineffective circuit transformations, achieving up to 3.1 times faster logic synthesis with comparable optimization performance.

paragraphs: Personalized ranking requires choosing which items to show and where to place them. Different users prefer different items, and an item's position can affect the response it receives. This paper models both influences and treats each complete ranked list as an action in a contextual bandit problem, where the platform learns from responses while trying to improve user satisfaction.

The algorithm adjusts predicted satisfaction using an upper confidence bound, allowing uncertainty to influence its choices. It then finds the list with the highest adjusted score through a maximum weight imperfect matching problem. This formulation matters because the number of possible lists grows exponentially with the candidate pool and list length, making direct treatment of every ranking as a separate action impractical.

Assuming responses follow a generalized linear model, the authors prove cumulative regret of order d times the square root of NKT. Here, d describes context dimension, N the candidate count, K the list length, and T the number of rounds. Experiments on simulated and real data also show improvement over the evaluated baseline.
icml-2024-adaptively-learning-to-select-.tldr: A contextual bandit ranking method uses confidence bounds and matching to personalize lists efficiently, with a regret guarantee under a generalized linear response model.

paragraphs: This paper asks when prior models or expert knowledge can help a learner become robust to adversarial perturbations. The learner receives a target training dataset and auxiliary hypotheses that initialize learning. The important question is how the robustness of that starting point affects the amount of target data needed to obtain useful guarantees.

The authors analyze an adversarial form of regularized empirical risk minimization, called A-RERM. With a nonnegative smooth loss and a strongly convex regularizer, they bound robust generalization error using both observed robust loss and initialization quality. If a weighted combination of the auxiliary hypotheses has small robust population loss, the bound achieves a fast rate of order 1/n. Otherwise, it has the standard order 1 divided by the square root of n.

The paper also bounds robust excess risk, with a slightly worse rate, and studies proximal stochastic adversarial training as a practical alternative. Its guarantee has the same sample-size dependence as A-RERM plus a perturbation-size-dependent term. These results make the value of transfer conditional on robust initialization quality.
icml-2024-adversarially-robust-hypothesi.tldr: Robust transfer learning can achieve faster generalization rates when auxiliary hypotheses provide a sufficiently good adversarially robust initialization.

paragraphs: Tree search can help a language model explore possible reasoning steps before choosing a continuation. Earlier approaches discussed here ask a pretrained model to judge how promising those steps are. That dependence becomes problematic when pretraining supplies too little knowledge for reliable judgments or when a solution requires planning far into the future.

TS-LLM introduces an AlphaZero-like learning framework with a learned value function. This function evaluates search possibilities, allowing search guidance to benefit from training within the relevant domain. The framework connects search to both decoding, when the model produces an answer, and training, when the model itself is improved. Its design is intended to accommodate different tasks, model sizes, and search depths.

The authors evaluate TS-LLM on reasoning, planning, alignment, and decision-making tasks. They report that it outperforms existing approaches and handles search trees reaching depth 64. These findings support the usefulness of learning search guidance rather than relying entirely on judgments available from pretraining. The training component also makes iterative model improvement part of the framework.
icml-2024-alphazero-like-tree-search-can.tldr: TS-LLM uses AlphaZero-like search with a learned value function to guide language-model generation and training, including searches reaching depth 64.

paragraphs: Maximal ancestral graphs represent causal relationships when hidden confounders and selection variables may be present. Observational data alone generally identify a Markov equivalence class rather than a single graph unless additional assumptions are made. Downstream analysis can therefore require listing all graphs in that class, preserving the causal possibilities that the observations do not distinguish.

The proposed algorithm constructs this list by recursively determining the local structure around each vertex. The authors characterize which local transformations are valid and provide sound and complete rules for incorporating them. These rules explicitly accommodate latent confounders and selection variables, so the construction respects the setting that makes maximal ancestral graphs useful.

The method outputs every graph in the equivalence class without redundancy. The authors further state that every intermediate graph generated by the recursive procedure is necessary for the listing task. This avoids the brute-force approach they identify as the previous available option. Empirical analysis supports improvements in efficiency and effectiveness, making systematic exploration of observationally indistinguishable causal graphs more practical.
icml-2024-an-efficient-maximal-ancestral.tldr: A recursive algorithm lists all maximal ancestral graphs in a Markov equivalence class without brute-force enumeration or redundant intermediate graphs.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning depends partly on which examples receive labels. Randomly labeling a fixed proportion can produce disappointing or unstable results, especially when each example has multiple views. This paper focuses on making that selection responsive to what the current classifiers find uncertain, rather than leaving the initial allocation of labels entirely to chance.

The method separates information shared across views from information specific to individual views. It builds two classifiers using existing labels and these decoupled sources of information. Examples classified with low confidence receive higher priority for labeling. Newly obtained labels then update the classifiers, allowing the next round of selection to reflect what has already been learned.

Selection and classifier updating alternate until classification performance is satisfactory. The approach therefore links the labeling process to an evolving model instead of treating labeling as a single preliminary step. Experiments on established benchmarks produce promising performance. The stated findings support combining shared and view-specific information to guide label acquisition, while the abstract does not claim a universal performance guarantee for this iterative strategy.
icml-2024-decouple-then-classify-a-dynam.tldr: An adaptive labeling strategy separates shared and view-specific information, prioritizes uncertain examples, and updates its classifiers as labels arrive.

paragraphs: Compositional understanding concerns how parts of a description or scene fit together, including attributes and relationships. This paper investigates why vision-language models can struggle with that ability. Its focus is the composition information represented inside the models and how weaknesses in those representations may help explain their reasoning failures.

The authors introduce evaluation methods grounded in a game-theoretic perspective. These methods assess vulnerability across different aspects of composition, including relations and attributes. Separating these aspects gives the investigation a more specific target than a single overall assessment of compositional ability: it asks which kinds of composition knowledge appear weak in the evaluated models.

Extensive experiments are reported to establish and validate insights into those weaknesses. The contribution is primarily diagnostic, offering evidence intended to guide later research on compositional reasoning. The abstract presents the evaluation approach as a way to investigate potential causes of limited understanding. Its practical significance is that a structured account of failure can help future work focus on the particular representations that need improvement.
icml-2024-diagnosing-the-compositional-k.tldr: Game-theoretic evaluations diagnose weaknesses in vision-language models' representations of compositional information, including attributes and relations.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often express actions through predefined text or JSON formats. The authors argue that these formats can restrict the available actions and make combining tools difficult. CodeAct instead uses executable Python as a common action format, allowing an agent to express operations through code that an interpreter can run.

The interpreter supplies observations that the agent can use in subsequent turns. The agent can revise earlier actions or produce new ones as the interaction develops. An analysis of 17 language models on API-Bank and a newly assembled benchmark finds that CodeAct improves on widely used alternatives, with success rates reported as up to 20% higher.

The paper also introduces CodeActInstruct, a dataset containing 7,000 multi-turn interactions, and CodeActAgent models fine-tuned from Llama2 and Mistral. Combining these interactions with existing training data improves agent-oriented performance without compromising general capability in the reported results. The resulting agents integrate a Python interpreter, use existing libraries for tasks such as model training, and can autonomously debug their code.
icml-2024-executable-code-actions-elicit.tldr: CodeAct gives language-model agents executable Python actions, improving evaluated task success and supporting multi-turn revision, library use, and self-debugging.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a decision-making system from demonstrations, but real demonstrations often contain imperfect behavior. The paper describes a difficulty with approaches that learn directly from such data: their performance guarantees typically depend on having some proportion of optimal examples. It investigates improving the demonstrations before using them for imitation learning.

The proposed purification procedure has two diffusion stages. A forward process adds noise, with the aim of smoothing the noise already present in imperfect demonstrations. A reverse generative process then reconstructs demonstrations from those diffused versions, seeking to recover optimal behavior. Imitation learning takes place after this purification step, so demonstration quality becomes an explicit target of the pipeline.

The theoretical analysis bounds the distance between purified and optimal demonstrations. That provides evidence for the approach without implying that purification always reconstructs an exactly optimal example. Experiments in MuJoCo and RoboSuite support its effectiveness from multiple perspectives. Together, the results motivate treating demonstration cleanup as a component of learning sequential behavior from imperfect examples.
icml-2024-imitation-learning-from-purifi.tldr: A diffusion-based purification step improves imperfect demonstrations before imitation learning, supported by a distance bound and experiments in MuJoCo and RoboSuite.

paragraphs: Combining models trained for separate tasks can reduce performance. This paper finds that task information can remain present after merging because different tasks mostly depend on different subsets of weights. The resulting perspective shifts attention toward locating and selectively using those subsets within a merged representation.

TALL-masks identify task-specific weight supports from a collection of task vectors. Applying these masks to a combined vector recovers more than 99% of single-task accuracy in the reported results, enabling compression of individual checkpoints. Studying mask intersections also reveals weights useful exclusively to one task and weights irrelevant to all tasks that nevertheless harm fusion. The authors call these selfish and catastrophic weights, respectively.

Consensus Merging removes such weights to improve existing merging methods. Experiments across vision and language benchmarks, involving up to 20 tasks, show consistent improvements to the evaluated approaches. A reported compression result reduces storage from 57Gb to 8.2Gb while retaining 99.7% of original performance. These findings connect selective weight use to both better merging and more compact checkpoint storage.
icml-2024-localizing-task-information-fo.tldr: TALL-masks locate retained task information in merged weights, enabling checkpoint compression and a consensus-based method that improves model merging.

paragraphs: BiLipNet is an invertible neural network designed to control two complementary properties. Lipschitzness limits how strongly outputs respond to input changes, while inverse Lipschitzness controls how distinguishable different inputs remain through their outputs. Having smooth control over both properties provides a way to shape a network's sensitivity while preserving an invertible mapping.

The architecture combines a new invertible residual layer with orthogonal layers. The residual layer has certified strong monotonicity and Lipschitzness, established using incremental quadratic constraints. The authors report that these certificates give substantially tighter bounds than spectral normalization. The contribution therefore includes both the network construction and a method for certifying its mathematical behavior.

PLNet composes BiLipNet with a quadratic potential to produce a scalar output. It satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and can learn nonconvex surrogate losses with a unique, efficiently computable global minimum. Computing BiLipNet's inverse, and consequently PLNet's minimum, is formulated as a sequence of three-operator splitting problems. This connects the architectural guarantees to available fast solution algorithms.
icml-2024-monotone-bi-lipschitz-and-poly.tldr: BiLipNet controls an invertible network's sensitivity and distinguishability, while PLNet uses it to construct nonconvex losses with a unique, efficiently computable global minimum.

paragraphs: Online change-point detection looks for changes as a stream of observations arrives. This paper addresses streams whose observations lie on a Riemannian manifold, a space with geometry that ordinary Euclidean methods do not respect. The authors argue that ignoring this structure makes existing Euclidean approaches unsuitable for the setting they study.

Their nonparametric algorithm monitors a generalized Karcher mean, a notion of a center adapted to the manifold's geometry. It computes this quantity through stochastic Riemannian optimization. The central design choice is therefore to track a geometric summary using updates that account for the space in which the observations live.

The paper provides theoretical bounds for detection and false-alarm performance. These rely on a new finite-sample convergence result for stochastic Riemannian gradient descent, linking the accuracy of the optimization procedure to the detector's behavior. Applications to two different manifolds, using synthetic and real data, illustrate the method's performance. The contribution joins a streaming detection algorithm with analysis that explicitly incorporates the geometry of its data.
icml-2024-non-parametric-online-change-p.tldr: A nonparametric streaming detector tracks a manifold-aware mean and provides theoretical bounds on detection and false alarms.

paragraphs: This paper studies online convex optimization when feedback arrives late and the environment changes over time. Performance is measured by dynamic regret against a sequence of comparison decisions. The sequence's path length measures how much those decisions move, making it possible to express the difficulty of tracking a changing target.

The first algorithm, DOGD, takes a gradient descent step whenever a delayed gradient arrives, following arrival order. Under mild assumptions, its regret scales with the square root of average delay times the horizon, multiplied by path length plus one. Its worst-case bound replaces average delay with maximum delay. Thus, even this simple update rule has guarantees that account for both delay and change.

An improved algorithm runs several DOGD instances with different learning rates and uses delayed performance to track the best one. It brings the path-length factor inside the square root in both bounds, improving the dependence on target movement. A matching lower bound establishes worst-case optimality for the improved algorithm, giving the result a theoretical benchmark beyond an upper-bound analysis alone.
icml-2024-non-stationary-online-convex-o.tldr: Combining delayed gradient-descent learners yields improved dynamic-regret bounds for changing environments and achieves worst-case optimality.

paragraphs: The paper studies identifying the better of two options with a fixed sampling budget and Bernoulli rewards. Its central result concerns universal improvement: no algorithm can match equal sampling on every problem instance while strictly improving on it for at least one instance. This establishes a precise boundary on attempts to dominate uniform sampling across all such A/B testing problems.

The proof introduces algorithms with consistency and stability properties. The authors show that any algorithm matching uniform sampling everywhere must belong to this class. They then derive an error-rate lower bound for the class and show that uniform sampling attains it. The conclusion does not say that another allocation can never perform better on a particular instance; it rules out doing so without losing somewhere else.

For more than two options, the paper provides initial results rather than the same complete characterization. It determines the asymptotic error rate of Successive Rejects and shows that uniform sampling performs better on some instances. This highlights why adaptive allocation alone does not establish universal superiority.
icml-2024-on-universally-optimal-algorit.tldr: For fixed-budget A/B testing with Bernoulli rewards, no algorithm can match uniform sampling on every instance and strictly beat it on another.

paragraphs: Automated prompt design often searches for one instruction to handle an entire task. This paper argues that a single instruction without demonstrations may not cover a complex task's full problem space. Mixture-of-Prompts instead divides that space into regions, each handled by an expert prompt containing both an instruction and demonstrations.

Construction proceeds in two phases. First, demonstrations are grouped into experts according to semantic similarity, motivated by a theoretical connection between in-context learning and kernel regression. Second, a region-based joint search chooses an instruction for each expert that complements its assigned demonstrations. The two components are designed together so that instructions and examples support the same specialized region.

Across several major benchmarks, the authors report an average win rate of 81% against prior approaches. This is a comparative win-rate result, rather than an assertion that the method answers 81% of all questions correctly. The findings support expanding prompt optimization beyond one universal instruction and using coordinated instruction-and-demonstration combinations to address variation within a task.
icml-2024-one-prompt-is-not-enough-autom.tldr: Mixture-of-Prompts automatically builds specialized instruction-and-demonstration experts, achieving an average 81% win rate against prior approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Random features make kernel methods more scalable, but much of their theory concerns ridge regression. This paper studies kernel quantile regression with random features, motivated by heterogeneous data and heavy-tailed noise. Quantile learning targets positions within an outcome distribution, making its statistical objective different from the ridge-regression setting that dominates existing analysis.

A central technical obstacle is the nonsmooth check loss used for quantile regression. The authors develop a refined error decomposition and connect the quantile estimator to kernel ridge regression with random features. Under mild conditions on the feature count, they establish learning rates that depend on the kernel space's capacity and are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors.

With data-dependent feature sampling, the theory also covers an agnostic setting in which the target quantile function need not belong exactly to the assumed kernel space. Modified assumptions extend the error analysis to Lipschitz continuous losses. Simulations and a real-data application support the theoretical findings, connecting scalable approximation to statistical guarantees beyond the usual ridge-regression objective.
icml-2024-optimal-kernel-quantile-learni.tldr: Kernel quantile regression with random features achieves capacity-dependent rates that are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors under the stated conditions.

paragraphs: Visual prompt tuning adapts pretrained vision models through learnable prompt tokens. Its performance can depend on prompt initialization and length, and it can struggle after self-supervised pretraining. This paper begins by examining how relationships between prompts and image patch tokens evolve during successful training, finding high mutual information between them.

That observation motivates initializing prompts from token prototypes drawn from the downstream task. The authors report that replacing the previous initialization this way substantially improves performance. They then streamline token construction into Self-Prompt-Tuning, or SPT, maintaining strong results with almost no additional computational expense relative to visual prompt tuning.

After MAE pretraining, the paper reports accuracy improvements over VPT of up to 10%–30%. The method also exceeds full fine-tuning in 19 of 24 cases while using less than 0.4% of learnable parameters. Experiments indicate robustness to prompt length and favorable scaling with model capacity and training-data size. These results suggest that how prompts are constructed and initialized can materially affect the usefulness of parameter-efficient visual adaptation.
icml-2024-revisiting-the-power-of-prompt.tldr: Initializing visual prompts from downstream token prototypes substantially improves adaptation, with strong reported results using very few learnable parameters.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning often emphasizes connections between nodes with similar features, an assumption called homophily. That can neglect useful connections between dissimilar nodes. Many methods also aggregate neighborhood information during inference, creating a deployment cost. S3GCL addresses both the diversity of graph relationships and the expense of using them at prediction time.

The authors first demonstrate a relationship between signal frequency and homophily. They then construct low-pass and high-pass graph filters using a cosine-parameterized Chebyshev polynomial. These filters produce views emphasizing different frequency content. An MLP encoder gains graph context through positive pairs formed from structurally and semantically neighboring nodes.

A contrastive objective connects the MLP's full-pass features with the graph network's filtered features. This cross-pass training removes the need for augmentation while supporting an inference approach based on the MLP. Experiments on real-world tasks show generalization across different homophily levels and improved inference efficiency. The method therefore uses graph structure during learning to support representations that are less costly to deploy.
icml-2024-s3gcl-spectral-swift-spatial-g.tldr: S3GCL combines spectral graph filtering with contrastive MLP training to handle varied homophily levels and improve inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Rendering a moving scene from a new viewpoint requires representing both appearance and change over time. The paper identifies quality and speed problems in approaches that combine a NeRF scene representation with a time-dependent deformation network. Superpoint Gaussian Splatting instead starts with explicit three-dimensional Gaussians to reconstruct the scene.

The method groups Gaussians with similar properties, such as rotation, translation, and location, into superpoints. These groups provide a representation for extending Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes with only a small additional computational cost. The grouping also gives the method stronger scene-manipulation capability, connecting its representation choice to more than image generation alone.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's practicality and effectiveness. The authors report state-of-the-art visual quality together with real-time rendering at high resolutions. These findings support superpoints as a way to preserve the rendering advantages of explicit Gaussians while accommodating motion. The reported combination of speed, quality, and manipulation capability is the main practical outcome of the framework.
icml-2024-superpoint-gaussian-splatting-.tldr: Grouping similar 3D Gaussians into superpoints enables high-quality dynamic-scene reconstruction with real-time high-resolution rendering.

paragraphs: Molecular conformer generation predicts three-dimensional arrangements of a molecule's atoms. This paper presents Molecular Conformer Fields, a diffusion approach trained directly on atomic positions. It avoids explicit structural modeling choices such as describing conformations through torsional angles, aiming to simplify the learning problem and make larger models straightforward to construct.

MCF represents a conformer as a function mapping elements of a molecular graph to locations in three-dimensional space. Generating conformers then becomes learning a distribution over these functions. The molecular graph remains part of the formulation, while the model learns spatial structure directly instead of relying on the particular handcrafted geometric assumptions highlighted by the authors.

The experiments report state-of-the-art results and substantial generalization gains as model capacity increases. These gains occur without enforcing inductive biases such as rotational equivariance. The finding supports scaling a simpler diffusion formulation as an effective approach in the evaluated setting. More broadly, the contribution shows how a function-based representation can turn molecular structure generation into a conceptually direct distribution-learning problem.
icml-2024-swallowing-the-bitter-pill-sim.tldr: Molecular Conformer Fields generate atomic coordinates through a scalable diffusion formulation, with larger models delivering strong reported generalization gains.

paragraphs: Random features offer a scalable approximation for kernel-based regression, but much of their theoretical support assumes independent, identically distributed observations. This paper asks what happens when observations are dependent. It analyzes kernel ridge regression with random features under two forms of dependence described through tau-mixing processes.

The distinction is how quickly the dependence coefficient decays: exponentially or polynomially. Under exponential decay, the authors prove minimax optimality, meaning the estimator attains the best worst-case rate for the analyzed setting. Under polynomial decay, their result is suboptimal. The analysis also makes explicit how the decay rate affects learning accuracy, rather than treating dependence as a single undifferentiated condition.

Numerical experiments on synthetic and real examples support the theoretical findings and the method's effectiveness for dependent data. The main implication is conditional: random-feature approximation can retain optimal statistical behavior under the specified exponential mixing conditions. The weaker polynomial-decay result shows that the established guarantee depends on the structure and persistence of dependence, not merely on using a scalable kernel approximation.
icml-2024-towards-theoretical-understand.tldr: Random-feature kernel ridge regression is minimax optimal under exponentially decaying tau-mixing dependence, while the polynomial-decay analysis yields a suboptimal rate.

paragraphs: Text detection systems often use separate models for different settings and scales, increasing computational and resource demands. Detect Any Text, or DAT, brings scene text detection, document layout analysis, and page detection into one end-to-end model. It handles text at word, line, paragraph, and page levels within this shared framework.

Its key component is interactive attention across granularities. Different text queries exchange structural information, helping the model learn representations that connect these levels. This allows detection at multiple scales to benefit mutually rather than treating each scale as a separate learning problem. A prompt-based segmentation module further refines the detected regions for curved text and complex layouts.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks for oriented and arbitrarily shaped scene text, document layouts, and page detection. These results support the combination of shared structural reasoning and segmentation refinement across distinct text-detection tasks. The practical contribution is a unified detection model whose components explicitly address both relationships between text scales and variation in the shapes of text regions.
icml-2024-towards-unified-multi-granular.tldr: DAT unifies word-to-page text detection through cross-granularity attention and segmentation refinement, reporting state-of-the-art results across multiple detection benchmarks.

paragraphs: Explaining predictions across different vision models and tasks can require repeated training and computation. This paper targets that repeated effort by developing a Transferable Vision Explainer, or TVE. The goal is to prepare an explainer that can be reused on downstream tasks without training it again on data specific to each task.

TVE obtains this transferability through pretraining on large datasets to learn what the authors call meta-attribution. Generic backbone encoders encode attribution knowledge for each input instance. This reusable representation is intended to support explanations across different downstream models and tasks, making pretraining the stage where broadly useful explanatory information is acquired.

The empirical study covers three vision-model architectures and three downstream datasets. Results indicate that TVE can effectively explain the evaluated tasks without additional downstream-data training. The finding supports transferring learned explanatory capability across the tested settings. It also connects the proposed representation to the practical goal of reducing repeated task-specific work when explanations are needed for multiple vision systems.
icml-2024-tve-learning-meta-attribution-.tldr: TVE pretrains reusable attribution knowledge to explain different vision models and tasks without additional training on downstream data.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how next-token pretraining might produce reasoning ability without explicit reasoning fine-tuning. It proposes viewing a language model as combining indirect reasoning paths encountered during training to derive new conclusions. The authors examine this perspective in two settings: logical reasoning over knowledge graphs and chain-of-thought reasoning.

They formalize reasoning paths as random walks through knowledge or reasoning graphs. Analysis of learned model distributions suggests that a weighted sum of relevant path probabilities can reasonably explain the models' reasoning behavior. This provides a mathematical way to connect exposure to individual paths during training with conclusions that depend on combining those paths.

Experiments and analyses across several knowledge-graph and chain-of-thought datasets explore the effects of training on random-walk paths. The results suggest that adding unlabeled reasoning paths can improve real-world multi-step reasoning. The paper therefore offers both an explanatory perspective and a possible training-data intervention. Its account is presented as supported and useful in the studied cases, rather than as a complete explanation of every form of language-model reasoning.
icml-2024-understanding-reasoning-abilit.tldr: Language-model reasoning can be usefully viewed as aggregating learned reasoning paths, and experiments suggest that adding unlabeled paths can improve multi-step reasoning.

paragraphs: A robot manipulating an object within its hand needs to estimate the object's pose. This paper addresses the shortage of large datasets for that problem by introducing VinT-6D, which combines vision, touch, and proprioception. Together, these modalities provide visual information, contact information, and information about the robot's own configuration for learning object-in-hand perception.

The dataset contains two million simulated entries and 100,000 real entries. Simulation data come from Mujoco and Blender, while a custom platform collects the real-world component. The resource is tailored to robotic hands, includes whole-hand tactile perception, and emphasizes high-quality alignment between modalities. The authors describe the real component as the largest of its kind to their knowledge.

A benchmark method built on VinT-6D shows significant performance improvements from combining modalities. This supports the usefulness of integrating the available sensory information for pose estimation. The real-data component is also intended to help bridge simulation and real-world use. The main contribution is therefore both a substantial multimodal resource and evidence that its combined sensing channels improve the evaluated method.
icml-2024-vint-6d-a-large-scale-object-i.tldr: VinT-6D supplies aligned visual, tactile, and proprioceptive data for object-in-hand pose estimation, with a benchmark showing gains from combining modalities.
